interest: SCAP returned black-market cases, 83 percent of provost dockets, to Japanese courts; also the first Supreme Court review vote.
overview: This file comprises State Department records from decimal file 894.041 (Judicial Branch of Government: National Courts in Japan) spanning September 1946 to March 1949. The earliest items (September and November 1946) represent documents concerning the Philippines (properly decimal 896.041) misfiled under Japan, reporting on the appointment of temporary justices of first instance to the Philippine Supreme Court to establish a quorum for collaboration trials (specifically the case of Jose P. Laurel) under Commonwealth Act No. 632, as well as an FBI background investigation of Clyde DeWitt. The substantive core of the file pertains to the reorganization, jurisdiction, and political role of the judiciary in Occupied Japan. Key documents include SCAPIN 1740 and Eighth Army Operational Directive No. 29/4 (June–August 1947), which transferred concurrent jurisdiction over black market and occupation-related property offenses from Allied military provost courts to Japanese courts under Imperial Ordinance No. 311; Staff Memorandum No. 55 (August 1947), regulating civil claims against United Nations nationals in Japanese courts; and an extensive diplomatic despatch (March 1949) analyzing the institutional standing and first constitutional popular review of the fourteen judges of the Supreme Court of Japan during the January 1949 general election.

subfiles.about: Transmits SCAPIN 1740 transferring criminal jurisdiction over occupation property offenses from military provost courts to Japanese courts.
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: POLAD Tokyo transmits SCAPIN 1740 (June 27, 1947), restoring Japanese court jurisdiction over unauthorized possession of occupation property to curb the black market.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1158 from POLAD Tokyo transmitting SCAPIN 1740 on Criminal Jurisdiction

subfiles.about: Transmits Eighth Army Operational Directive No. 29/4 detailing the division of jurisdiction and supervision over Japanese courts trying occupation-related offenses.
subfiles.from: Counselor of Mission, United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1253 encloses Eighth Army Operational Directive No. 29/4 (issued August 18, 1947 under Lt. Gen. Eichelberger), which provides detailed instructions for implementing SCAPIN 1740 and supervising Japanese courts. The directive defines offenses prejudicial to occupation objectives and stipulates that Japanese public procurators may only waive prosecution of such cases after obtaining approval from designated local Occupation Force court authorities. The enclosures include the English text of Imperial Ordinance No. 311, setting maximum penalties of ten years' imprisonment with hard labor or fines up to 75,000 yen for acts prejudicial to the occupation, along with a reference copy of SCAPIN 1740.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1253 from POLAD Tokyo transmitting Eighth Army Operational Directive No. 29/4

subfiles.about: Transmits GHQ SCAP Staff Memorandum No. 55 defining Japanese court jurisdiction over civil actions involving United Nations nationals.
subfiles.from: Counselor of Mission, United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: POLAD transmits Staff Memorandum No. 55 (August 11, 1947) defining Japanese courts' civil jurisdiction over United Nations nationals.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1271 from POLAD Tokyo transmitting Staff Memorandum No. 55 on Civil Actions

subfiles.about: Provides an extensive report on the Supreme Court of Japan, focusing on its early decisions and the first constitutional popular review of its judges.
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 193 provides a thorough overview of the Supreme Court of Japan during its first eighteen months under the 1947 Constitution, centered on the first popular review of judges held concurrently with the January 23, 1949 general election. All fourteen sitting judges were confirmed with an average dismissal vote of only 4.41 percent, although public unfamiliarity with voting procedures and general voter apathy were widely criticized; Chief Judge Tadahiko Mibuchi received the highest number of votes against retention due to his public prominence and ill health. The report examines the Japan Communist Party's opposition to the Court following its decision upholding the government's strike ban against public railway and communications workers, summarizes key constitutional jurisprudence regarding civil liberties and confessions under prolonged detention, and discusses emerging debates on whether to reform or abolish the popular review system.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 193 from POLAD Tokyo on the Supreme Court of Japan and Popular Review of Judges
